29.title: Three palaces
29.hook: one for the rains, one for winter, one for summer; "I was delicately nurtured" (AN 3.38)
29.howItsDone: Buddhists retell the Buddha's sheltered youth as the setting for his going forth; the Sukhamala Sutta, where he describes it, is studied as a teaching on the three intoxications of youth, health and life.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the swan, and the court that gave it to the boy who saved it. Your line was life belongs to who protects it. Day twenty-nine.
screen: `THE SWAN — LIFE BELONGS TO WHO PROTECTS IT.`

segments.voice: Remember Kondañña's one raised finger, and the king who hoped his son would stay home and rule? This is where the king acts on that hope. If the boy is going to leave because he sees the world's pain, the reasoning goes, then make sure he never sees it. Wrap him in so much comfort that he never has a reason to look past the garden wall. And for years, it works. Today, in the Buddha's own words, what it was like to grow up that way.
screen: `THE PALACE.` → `A FATHER'S PLAN.` → `SO MUCH COMFORT, NO REASON TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: In one of the discourses, the Buddha looks back on his youth. He says he was raised delicately. His father had lotus ponds made just for him, one of blue lotuses, one of red, one of white. His clothes were made of cloth from Kasi, the country around Benares. A white parasol was held over him day and night, so that cold and heat, dust and grass and dew wouldn't touch him. And he had three palaces. One for the cold season, one for the hot season, one for the rainy season. During the four months of rain, he says, he stayed up in the rainy-season palace, surrounded by musicians, and never once came down. Even the servants in his father's house ate fine rice and meat, where in other houses servants got broken rice and sour gruel. No humble origin story: he grew up rich, and he says so. But then, in the same passage, the tone changes. He says: amid all that, a thought came to him. Ordinary, untaught people see someone old, and they're disgusted, forgetting that they'll grow old too. The same with sickness. The same with death. And when he saw that, he says, the pride of youth, the pride of health, the pride of being alive, all fell away from him. The three palaces kept out the rain, the heat, the cold. They couldn't keep out that thought. Comfort isn't a bad thing. But it can be a wall. And walls, sooner or later, have gates.

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, then look around for one comfort you forgot you had: a roof in the rain, warm water from a tap, a chair that holds you, glasses that let you see. Notice it the way the Buddha noticed his palaces, and feel a little gratitude for it. Then gently ask: is there anything it's keeping me from seeing? You don't need an answer; let the question sit beside the gratitude.
Three palaces. One for the cold, one for the heat, one for the rains: the comfort the Buddha grew up in, and the thought that got through anyway.

30.title: Yasodhara
30.hook: the marriage; in the stories she is his equal, and later a nun in her own right
30.tomorrow: The first sight: an old man
30.howItsDone: Buddhists remember Yasodhara as the Buddha's wife and the mother of Rahula, and in many traditions as a nun and arahant; her story is told in temple art, festivals and verse, and some communities honor her especially as a model of steadfast practice.

screen: `DAY THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: three palaces, and a thought about age, sickness and death that got through the walls. Your line: comfort can be a wall. Today, the woman beside him.
screen: `THREE PALACES — COMFORT CAN BE A WALL.`

segments.voice: At sixteen, the tellings say, the prince is married to a beautiful young woman of the Sakya clan. Some versions even have a contest of skill. In a lot of old stories, that's where the princess stops: a prize, handed over at the end like a trophy. She barely speaks. No one tells us what she thought. Keep reading this one, though, and she refuses to stay a trophy. She has a name, a history of her own, and a path that becomes hers.
screen: `A MARRIAGE AT SIXTEEN.` → `IN OLD STORIES, THE PRINCESS IS A PRIZE.` → `SHE REFUSES TO STAY A TROPHY.`

segments.voice: Her name is Yasodhara. Yasa means glory or fame; dhara, one who bears or holds. She who bears glory. The first surprise: the oldest texts barely name her. The monastic rules usually just call her Rahula's mother, after the son she'll soon have. It's the later tellings that bring her forward, and they make her his equal. The commentaries say she was born on the same day as him. The Jataka stories say the two were together across many past lives, and that long ago, when the future Buddha first vowed to seek awakening, she vowed to walk beside him, life after life. Not a prize he won. A partner who chose. Her story doesn't end with the marriage, or with his leaving, which is a few days away. Years after he begins teaching, Yasodhara leaves the palace too. She joins the order of nuns, and the tradition remembers her as fully awakened, an arahant, in her own right. There are verses said to be hers, looking back on her long journey. Different Buddhist communities tell her story in different ways, and some modern writers retell the whole life from her side; the old sources leave a lot unsaid. But the tradition that kept her remembered her as more than a wife left behind. She walked the same path, and reached the same end.

31.title: The first sight: an old man
31.hook: on a chariot ride with Channa he sees a man bent with age and asks, will this happen to me
31.carry: this is coming for all of us
31.tomorrow: the second sight: a sick man
31.howItsDone: Buddhists retell the four sights as the beginning of the Buddha's search, and one's own aging is the first of the five remembrances, which the Buddha said should be reflected on often.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yasodhara, she who bears glory, the prince's partner and later a nun in her own right. Your line: partner, not prize. Today, the road out of the palace.
screen: `YASODHARA — PARTNER, NOT PRIZE.`

segments.voice: A road swept clean and hung with decorations. And at the side of it, a man who was never supposed to be there. The stories say the young prince grew up without a single old face. His father, remembering the prophecy that his son might leave and become a teacher, kept every sad thing out of sight: three palaces, music, gardens, young and beautiful people everywhere. Then one day the prince asks his charioteer, Channa, to drive him out to the park. This is the first of four things he was never meant to see.
screen: `A ROAD SWEPT CLEAN.` → `A PALACE WITH NO OLD FACES.` → `A MAN BY THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The man is bent almost double. Gray hair, few teeth, leaning on a stick, trembling as he walks. The prince has never seen anything like him. What's wrong with that man, the prince asks. His hair isn't like other people's. His body isn't like other bodies. Channa answers plainly: that's what we call an old man. Then the question the story turns on. Will this happen to me? Channa doesn't soften it. Yes. To you, to me, to everyone. Nobody gets past old age. The prince has the chariot turned around. No park today. He goes home and sits alone with it. One wrinkle in the sources: the Pali discourses tell the four sights about Vipassi, a Buddha of long ago. Later biographies tell it of Siddhattha, and that's the version in temples and picture books today. It echoes the Buddha's own quieter memory from the palaces: the pride of youth falling away. Either way, the point holds. The prince didn't learn a new fact; everyone knows people grow old. What changed is that he let it mean him. Old age stopped being something that happens to other people. That shift, from them to me, is where Buddhists say the path begins to open.

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and bring to mind one old face you know well: the lines around the eyes, the hands. Let a quiet thought arrive: this face was once young like mine, and mine is on its way to this. Hold the two faces side by side, kindly, and let any gratitude come.

32.title: The second sight: a sick man
32.hook: a man shaking with fever by the road; and this too, he asks
32.tomorrow: the third sight: a dead man
32.howItsDone: The five remembrances Buddhists reflect on include being subject to illness, and in some traditions monks visit and chant for the sick.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Channa drove him to the first sight: an old man by the road, and the prince asking, will this happen to me. Your line was this is coming for all of us. Day thirty-two.
screen: `CHANNA — THIS IS COMING FOR ALL OF US.`

segments.voice: Something is off the moment you wake. A scratch in the throat, a heaviness behind the eyes. Yesterday you had plans. Today the plans belong to the fever. The stories say the prince went out a second time. The king had doubled the guards and the music, hoping to keep his son's mind on pleasure. Channa drove the chariot out again, down a road swept clean. And by the side of it lay a man shaking with fever, too weak to stand, being helped up by others. The prince looked, and asked the question again, a little quieter this time.
screen: `THE MORNING YOU WAKE UP SICK.` → `A SECOND RIDE.` → `A MAN SHAKING BY THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: What's wrong with him, the prince asks. Channa tells him: this man is sick. And again the question: can this happen to me? And again the plain answer: nobody is beyond sickness. The first sight was about time, the slow bending of age. This one is sharper. Sickness doesn't wait for old age. It can arrive at twenty, at five, on a Tuesday, in the middle of your plans. The prince had thought of his body as his, the way a palace was his. The fever by the road said otherwise. Years later, the Buddha put it in one line. This body, he told his monks, isn't yours, and it doesn't belong to anyone else either. It's the result of old causes, something to be seen clearly, not owned. The body is borrowed. Not a prison, not a possession. A loan, looked after for a while, returned in the end. And the Buddha lived what he taught. Near the end of his life, sick and in pain, he told his friend Ananda that his body was like an old cart that keeps going only because it's held together with straps. He didn't pretend. He didn't despair either. Buddhists say this is the point: to see sickness as it is, without the extra layer of shock, why me, how dare you. The fever is real. The outrage is the part you might be able to set down.

segments.voice: Settle into your seat and look for one small ache: a stiff neck, a sore knee, tired eyes. Rest your attention on it gently, the way you'd rest a hand on a friend's shoulder. Notice it without the story, not 'this always happens,' not 'why won't it stop,' just the sensation itself: warm, tight, dull, moving. If the ache changes, let it; if your mind runs off, come back to it.
Vyādhi. Sickness, the Pali word for the fever that stops the prince on the road and comes to everyone, at any age, without asking.

segments.voice: Your line: the body is borrowed. Nobody owns one outright, not even a prince. Until tomorrow.

33.title: The third sight: a dead man
33.hook: a funeral procession, the mourners weeping; the prince goes quiet
33.howItsDone: In many Buddhist monasteries the five remembrances are chanted regularly, and Buddhists often reflect on death (maranasati) as a regular practice, sometimes at funerals where monks chant on impermanence.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: vyādhi, a man shaking with fever, and the prince learning sickness comes at any age. Your line: the body is borrowed. Today, the third ride.
screen: `VYĀDHI — THE BODY IS BORROWED.`

segments.voice: Most of us remember a first funeral. The smell of the flowers. Shoes that pinched. An adult you'd never seen cry, crying. Something in the room could not be fixed. The prince had never had that day. Now Channa's chariot meets a crowd coming the other way, in mourning clothes, weeping, some beating their chests. On their shoulders, a bier. On the bier, a man wrapped in cloth, perfectly still. The prince watches them pass, and for a while says nothing.
screen: `YOUR FIRST FUNERAL.` → `A CROWD COMING THE OTHER WAY.` → `THE PRINCE GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: When he asks, the question is simple. What is that? Channa says: a dead man. He won't see his mother or father again, and they won't see him. Will I die too? Yes. Everyone. Old age was slow. Sickness was sudden. Death is final. In the old stories he rides home shaken, and in some tellings cries out that it's shameful to be born, if this is where birth leads. The third sight adds something. It isn't only about my death. The mourners are the other half of the scene. Everyone we love will go, and we will go from them. That's why it hits hardest. A practice grows straight from this moment. The Buddha taught five things to reflect on often, and many monasteries chant them. I'm of the nature to grow old. I'm of the nature to become sick. I'm of the nature to die. Everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I'll be parted from them. My actions are the only thing I truly own. It can sound bleak. The teaching points the other way: not darker, vivid. The phone call you meant to make. The person across the kitchen table, who won't always be there. The Pali word for death is marana, and the Buddha's teaching is that looking at it calmly is how you stop wasting the time you have.

34.title: The fourth sight: a wanderer
34.hook: a shaven man in a robe, owning nothing, calm
34.carry: there is another way to live
34.howItsDone: Buddhist monks and nuns today still follow the samana's way of life in many places, shaving their heads, wearing robes and receiving food as alms, and lay Buddhists often honor them as living examples of another way to live.

screen: `MARANA — EVERYONE WE LOVE WILL GO.`

segments.voice: A shaved head. A plain robe the color of earth. A bowl, and as far as anyone can tell, nothing else. Three rides have brought three shocks: age, sickness, death. If the story stopped there, it would be a very sad one, and the prince might have hidden in his gardens for life. But on a fourth ride, more troubled than he has ever been, he sees this man walking along the road. And his face is calm. Not cheerful, not grim. Calm, in a world that just showed the prince three reasons to despair.
screen: `A SHAVED HEAD, A BOWL, A ROBE.` → `THREE RIDES, THREE SHOCKS.` → `A CALM FACE.`

segments.voice: Who is that, the prince asks. Channa says: a samana. A wanderer, one who has gone forth. The word comes from a root meaning to strive, to make an effort. The Buddha's India had many of them: men, and some women, who left home, gave up property and family life, and walked the roads seeking answers to exactly the prince's questions. Why do we age? Why do we suffer? Is there a way out? They lived on what people put in their bowls, slept in forests and caves, and debated each other in public halls. They weren't one group; there were many teachers and many paths. The Jains, whose tradition is still alive today, came from this same world. So did the Buddha: for the rest of his life, outsiders would call him the samana Gotama. Here's the heart of the fourth sight. The first three were questions. The fourth was a possibility. Age, sickness and death come for everyone, palace or no palace. And here was someone who had looked at the same facts and was not afraid. The stories say something in the prince went still and bright. Not an answer yet. Just the sense that there is another way to live, and someone is already living it. That's where his search begins.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the calmest face you have ever seen: a teacher, a grandparent, a stranger on a train, even a statue. Notice the eyes, the mouth, the shoulders. Then let your own face do a little of the same: soften the jaw, rest the eyes, and let calm be possible for a minute.
Samana. A wanderer, one who strives: someone who has left home to seek the truth. The fourth sight, and the first hope.

35.title: A son is born
35.hook: news of his son arrives; the child is named Rahula, "a fetter"
35.carry: love, and the fear inside it
35.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the story of Rahula's birth as part of the going forth, and Buddhist parents are taught to love fully while practicing non-attachment, which means not clinging, rather than not caring.

screen: `DAY THIRTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth sight: a samana, a calm wanderer with a bowl. Your line: there is another way to live. Today, the last day in the palace week.
screen: `SAMANA — THERE IS ANOTHER WAY TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: A messenger is hurrying down the road with news from the palace. In the stories, the prince is riding home from the park, the fourth sight still shining in his mind, when the messenger reaches him. Yasodhara has given birth. You have a son. New parents sometimes describe two things arriving at once: a love bigger than they expected, and right behind it, the fear of losing what they love. The prince, the stories say, answers with a strange sentence. Not a cheer. Something closer to a sigh.
screen: `A MESSENGER ON THE ROAD.` → `YOU HAVE A SON.` → `NOT A CHEER. A SIGH.`

segments.voice: What the prince says, in the later telling, is: a rahula is born, a fetter is born. A bond. Something that ties me down. The king hears it and names the baby Rahula. It sounds harsh to modern ears, and people read it more than one way. Some hear a father torn: he has just glimpsed another way to live, and now a child holds him to this one. Others hear plain honesty about love. He doesn't say the baby is bad. He says the love is binding. Some scholars add that the name may once have meant something else, perhaps tied to Rahu, the shadow that swallows the moon in an eclipse, and the fetter story may explain a name that came first. The timing differs too. In the Pali commentaries, Rahula is born the day his father leaves. In some northern Buddhist tellings, he's born years later, on the night of the awakening. The sources disagree, and that's fine to say. Underneath it all is a feeling: love, and the fear inside it. Buddhism doesn't say stop loving. It says look closely at the gripping, the part that wants to hold so tight nothing can ever change. And Rahula doesn't vanish from the story. He comes back, and the Buddha himself will teach him. Now look back at this week: three palaces, Yasodhara, four sights, and a son. Everything the prince has, and everything he is about to leave.
screen: `A RAHULA IS BORN — A FETTER.` · `A FATHER TORN, OR PLAIN HONESTY?` · `THE SOURCES DISAGREE.` · `LOVE WITHOUT GRIPPING.` · then, large: `LOVE, AND THE FEAR INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Hold something you love in your hand: a mug, a photo, a stone from a beach, or simply your own other hand. Close your fingers tight around it for a breath or two and feel the tension climb your arm. Then slowly loosen until it rests in an open palm, still yours, still loved, just not squeezed, and breathe with the difference between holding and gripping.
Rahula. The Buddha's son, whose name, in the old telling, means a fetter: the tie of love that holds us.
screen: `RAHULA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: love, and the fear inside it. Loosening the grip is not letting go of the love. The palace week, done.
